# Independent audit: geometric mode and saturated-positive comparison

Audited source:
`candidate a6e6fd61fe60c16a`.


The result is a scalar theorem for saturated positive coefficients. It
does not establish a reduction of arbitrary bounded coefficient patterns,
simplex normals, or mixed-integer sources to that domain.

## Conditional means and the discrete mode bound

The Toeplitz proof of convolution log-concavity is valid. For increasing
row and column indices, the first diagonal product uses two middle
indices, while the other product uses their two extremes with the same
sum. Decreasing successive ratios give the required minor inequality,
including the zero extension. In each product-matrix minor all potentially
nonzero intermediate indices lie in a finite interval, so Cauchy--Binet
has no infinite-series interchange.

For the conditional law of N_i, the claimed likelihood-ratio inequality
reduces to

    r(a+1) r(b)>=r(a) r(b+1), a=n-v<b=n-u,

which has the correct log-concavity orientation. The conditional supports
at n and n+1 obey the same inequality after zero extension. Moreover

    E_(g_(n+1)) j-E_(g_n) j
     =sum_(u<v)(v-u)[g_(n+1)(v)g_n(u)-g_(n+1)(u)g_n(v)],

so its nonnegativity follows without invoking an unproved monotone
coupling. Summing the conditional means gives n, which proves that their
nonnegative increments sum to one and individually do not exceed one.

I independently rederived the geometric Stein identity by shifting its
single-variable series while conditioning on all other variables. With
lambda=b/(1+b), its coefficient of phi(m) on the right is
b[m p(m-1)-(m+1)p(m)]=(m-b)p(m), as required. Summing and evaluating at
phi=1_{N=n} yields exactly

    tau(n-1)p(n-1)=[tau(n)+n-mu]p(n).

For n<=mu-b_max, the bracket is at most tau(n-1), since the tau increment
is at most b_max. It is strictly positive by the recurrence and p(n)>0.
Thus division gives p(n)>=p(n-1), with the stated orientation. No assertion
about a mode of an arbitrary log-concave law is being substituted for this
geometric calculation.

## Gamma-density derivative and coefficient transfer

For k>=2 the gamma density, extended by zero on the negative halfline, is
globally Lipschitz. At k=2 it has a derivative jump at zero, but Y>0 almost
surely under the stated sum condition. Difference quotients are therefore
dominated and converge almost surely, justifying

    f'(0)=E[g_k'(Y)].

Exponential tilting changes each positive phase mean b_i to
lambda_i=b_i/(1+b_i), with factor L=product(1+b_i)^(-1). The complete
homogeneous moment identity has the factorial r!, so the two derivative
terms reduce precisely to L(h_(k-2)-h_(k-1)), with no missing factor of k.
The associated geometric sum has mu=sum b_i>=k and b_max<=1; hence
k-1<=mu-b_max, and the discrete mode bound applies at exactly the needed
index. This proves f'(0)<=0.

For the probability P_k, differentiation of gamma survival gives
-E[E_i g_k(E_0+sum b_l E_l)]. Size bias replaces E_i by E_i+E_i', yielding

    partial_i P_k=-f_(V-b_i E_i')(0).

For an independent negative exponential convolution W=X-bE', direct
integration by parts gives

    -b f_W'+f_W=f_X.

Taking W=V-b_i E_i'-b_j E_j', the density appearing in partial_i removes
the EXTRA j phase and therefore equals f_W-b_j f_W'. Similarly the
density in partial_j equals f_W-b_i f_W'. Subtracting the two negative
densities gives exactly

    partial_i P_k-partial_j P_k=-(b_i-b_j)f_W'(0).

This is the potentially delicate sign; it is correct. In the displayed
notation f_(W+bE') in the source, the phase being added back is the same
phase subtracted in defining W, not a new independent positive phase.
The proof uses it in that correct sense.

The total negative coefficient sum of W is k+b_i+b_j, and every coefficient
is at most one, including the original distinguished coefficient of one.
The density-derivative theorem therefore applies. When b_i>=b_j, the
partial_i-minus-partial_j difference is nonnegative. Moving mass from
i to j lowers the probability as long as the order is retained.

Choosing an above-average and a below-average coordinate and stopping
when one reaches the common average preserves both their order and the
box constraints. Each step fixes at least one additional coordinate;
there are finitely many steps. The case q=k-1 is already the all-one
vector. Boundary zero coefficients are handled by the stated convex
combination with the positive equal vector. The comparison event has
zero equality probability because the independent gamma variable has a
density, so the almost-sure coefficient limit permits bounded convergence.

## Arbitrarily many phases and the explicit limit

Padding the equal q-vector with a zero coordinate and applying the
q+1-coordinate theorem proves the claimed decreasing direction. The
mean and variance of ((k-1)/q)Gamma(q) are exactly k-1 and (k-1)^2/q.
The threshold trapping argument therefore proves convergence to the
probability at the constant k-1. It does not interchange a nonuniform
integral limit or require almost-sure convergence of the entire sequence.

For s>=0 a direct integration gives

    Pr(Gamma(k)>=E_0+s)
      =e^(-s) sum_(j=0)^(k-1) s^j/j! [1-2^(j-k)].

At s=k-1 this is precisely the source formula. In particular the values
5/(4e) and 27/(8e^2) for k=2,3 are correct. The separate k=1 case gives
Pr(E_1>=E_0)=1/2.

No step above requires strict coefficient inequalities at the final
statement, a nonsaturated positive-coefficient reduction, or a numerical
estimate of the sequence G_k.
